17 On a planet, a gravitational force F acts on a mass of 6.0 kg. The mass is moved by force F a
distance of 30 m in the direction of the gravitational field. The work done by the field is 450 J.
What is the force F on the mass and what is the acceleration of free fall g on the planet?
F / N
g / m s–2
A
0.067
0.011
B
0.067
0.40
C
15
2.5
D
15
90

hints: Notice the $450\text{ J}$ of work is done by the $F$ acting through $30\text{ m}$ in the same direction as the field, so $W = Fd$ applies with no angle factor.
Connect that work relation to weight on the planet: once $F$ is known, use $F = mg$ with $m = 6.0\text{ kg}$ to find $g$.
First calculate $F = W/d = 450/30$ in $\text{N}$, then calculate $g = F/m$ in $\text{m s}^{-2}$ and match both columns.
walkthrough: Identify the given data: mass $m = 6.0\text{ kg}$, displacement in direction of force $d = 30\text{ m}$, work done by gravitational force $W = 450\text{ J}$.
State the work rule for force parallel to displacement: $W = Fd$. Rearrange for force: $F = W/d$.
Substitute with units: $F = 450\text{ J} / 30\text{ m} = 15\text{ N}$. This eliminates the rows with $0.067\text{ N}$.
State the weight rule on the planet: gravitational force $F = mg$, so acceleration of free fall $g = F/m$.
Substitute: $g = 15\text{ N} / 6.0\text{ kg} = 2.5\text{ m s}^{-2}$. Units check: $\text{N kg}^{-1}$ is the same as $\text{m s}^{-2}$.
The pair $F = 15\text{ N}$ and $g = 2.5\text{ m s}^{-2}$ matches the table row. This is option C.

A.explanation: This inverts the work relation as $F = 30/450$ and then divides again by mass, giving $0.067\text{ N}$ and $0.011\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

B.explanation: This uses $F = 30/450 = 0.067\text{ N}$ instead of $W/d$, and then multiplies by $6.0\text{ kg}$ to get $0.40\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

C.explanation: Work $W = Fd$ gives $F = 450/30 = 15\text{ N}$, and weight $F = mg$ gives $g = 15/6.0 = 2.5\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

D.explanation: Force $F = 15\text{ N}$ is correct but $g$ multiplies by mass as $15 \times 6.0 = 90\text{ m s}^{-2}$ instead of dividing by mass.
